subject: feat(table): add Transaction.AssertRefSnapshotID (Java UpdateRequirements parity) (#1786)
body:
* fix(table): reject conflicting same-ref assertions and build ref requirements from the base state

Transaction.apply deduplicated assert-ref-snapshot-id requirements by
(type, ref) but silently kept the first when two assertions for the
same ref required different snapshot ids. Both can never hold against
the catalog: keeping either silently drops a check the caller
registered, so reject the pair at apply time with a named error
instead of a confusing catalog rejection. Only requirements actually
appended are validated against the staged metadata — a deduplicated
twin re-asserts base state the staged metadata has intentionally
moved past; its kept twin was validated when first added.

Snapshot producers built their assertion from the staged metadata's
current snapshot. For the second producer commit in one transaction
that is an intermediate snapshot the catalog has never seen, which
the new conflict check would correctly reject (previously masked by
dedup silently keeping the first assertion). Producers now assert the
BASE table's branch head — the catalog state the writer actually
read, and the only assertion that can hold at commit time. This
matches Java's UpdateRequirements, which accumulates one assertion
per ref built from the base table state.

RollbackToSnapshot and ExpireSnapshots built their assertions from
the staged refs the same way and are moved to base-state requirements
too; refs staged by the transaction itself (absent on the base) get
no assertion from them, since the update that created such a ref
already carries its own base-state requirement.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* feat(table): add Transaction.AssertRefSnapshotID for compare-and-swap commits

Metadata-only transactions (e.g. exactly-once bookkeeping that records
ingestion progress in table properties) cannot detect that the branch
changed between their read and their commit: the branch assertion
Commit builds implicitly is rewritten to the fresh head between
retries and the commit is replayed, so two such committers silently
interleave and the later one clobbers the earlier one's properties.
Expose the existing requirement so a committer can require that the
branch is unchanged from the head it read:

    func (t *Transaction) AssertRefSnapshotID(branch string) error

An empty branch defaults to the transaction's target branch; a branch
that does not exist on the base is required to stay absent. The
requirement asserts the BASE table's branch head — the same state
snapshot producers assert, matching Java's UpdateRequirements — so an
explicit requirement and a producer-built one for the same branch
collapse to one regardless of registration order. The branch is
marked pinned before the requirement becomes visible so a concurrent
Commit can never observe the assertion without its pinned status.

doCommit's refresh-and-replay must not rewrite these explicit
assertions to the fresh head between retries — the caller asked for
compare-and-swap semantics — so pinned branches are exempted from
rewriteRefSnapshotRequirements, and once the refreshed metadata shows
a pinned assertion can no longer hold the commit fails fast with
ErrCommitFailed instead of burning the remaining retries.

The empty-append test pins the workaround this API replaces: an empty
AddFiles commits a legal empty snapshot that moves the branch head
(Java newFastAppend().commit() parity), which writers can use to
serialize metadata-only commits through a producer's assertion at the
cost of an empty snapshot per commit.

subject: feat(table): RowDelta.RemoveDeletes for deletion-vector supersession (#1785)
body:
* feat(table): add Positions iterator to RoaringPositionBitmap

RoaringPositionBitmap exposes Set, Contains, and Cardinality but no way
to enumerate the positions it holds. Consumers that need the contents
of an existing deletion vector (e.g. to merge it into a superseding DV,
as the v3 spec requires when a data file's DV is replaced) currently
have to Serialize() the bitmap and re-parse the Iceberg portable wire
format by hand.

Add Positions() iter.Seq[uint64], yielding every set position in
ascending 64-bit order. The yielded values are the same ones passed to
Set, mirroring Java's RoaringPositionBitmap#forEach.

Tests cover the empty bitmap, a single position above the 32-bit
boundary, ascending order across multiple bitmap keys with agreement
against Cardinality, and early termination by the consumer.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* feat(table): support deletion vector supersession in RowDelta

The v3 spec allows at most one live deletion vector per data file. A
writer adding a DV for a data file that already carries one must write
a DV containing the previous DV's positions and remove the previous DV
entry in the same snapshot. Java's RowDelta supports this through
removeDeletes; the Go RowDelta could only add delete files, forcing
consumers into a two-snapshot ReplaceFiles + RowDelta workaround whose
intermediate snapshot briefly resurrects the previously deleted rows.
The engine-internal merge-on-read delete path already supersedes DVs
this way (writePositionDeletesForFiles); this exposes the same
capability to library users who write their own deletion vectors.

Add RowDelta.RemoveDeletes(files ...iceberg.DataFile), mirroring Java's
RowDelta#removeDeletes, restricted to deletion vectors. Removal
identity is (file path, referenced data file), not path alone: a
multi-blob Puffin file legally carries DVs for several data files under
one path, one manifest entry each, and superseding one blob must not
drop its siblings' entries. The snapshot producer's existing
removeDeletionVector plumbing already keys removals this way, so only
the matching entry is recorded as DELETED while other live entries at
the same Puffin path survive.

Commit first resolves every removed file to its live entry in the
current snapshot's delete manifests — when several live entries share
the removed file's path, its referenced data file selects among them,
and the removal is rejected as ambiguous if it does not identify
exactly one — then validates against the RESOLVED entries, never the
caller's copies, so a stale or forged DataFile with a real path but a
wrong referenced_data_file cannot pair a removal with an unrelated
replacement:

  - every resolved entry must be a DV (Puffin pos-delete with
    referenced_data_file); expunging plain pos/eq-delete files remains
    the rewrite path's job,
  - every removed DV's referenced data file — as recorded by the live
    entry — gets a replacement DV among the added delete files, so a
    delta cannot silently resurrect rows (content coverage stays the
    writer's responsibility, as in Java),
  - a removed file that does not resolve to a live delete entry is an
    error, as are two removals resolving to live entries that reference
    the same data file (the producer keys DV removals by referenced
    data file, and two live DVs on one data file is a spec violation to
    surface, not paper over); the DELETED record is produced from the
    manifest's own entry so it keeps its spec ID, partition, and
    sequence numbers. Blob offset and size are not part of the
    identity: the spec's one live DV per data file makes (path,
    referenced data file) unique among live entries, and every produced
    record comes from the live entry, so stale caller-side offsets are
    harmless.

When removals are present the delta commits through the overwrite
producer, which already drops removed entries from inherited delete
manifests and records them with status DELETED; the overwrite
producer's default conflict validator is suppressed in favor of
RowDelta's own, the same way rewrites do. Without removals the
fast-append path is unchanged.

Also correct the stale comments on commitOpts.validators and RowDelta
claiming pre-flight validators run only on the first attempt; doCommit
runs them on every attempt of the retry loop against the freshly
refreshed catalog state.

The end-to-end test builds a v3 table with a live DV, commits a
superseding RowDelta, and asserts single-snapshot shape (operation
delete, added and removed delete file counts), exactly one live DV
with the superseded entry marked DELETED, and row visibility at plan
level (the scanner plans only the replacement DV and its bitmap hides
the union of positions) and through materialized Arrow records. A
shared multi-blob Puffin test supersedes one of two DVs sharing a
Puffin path and asserts the sibling entry stays live (its rows still
hidden) alongside the DELETED record for the same path, plus
superseding both blobs in one delta. Validation failures are covered
for a missing replacement, a non-DV live entry behind a DV-shaped
caller copy, a forged reference targeting an unrelated DV, stale
caller metadata pairing correctly per the live entry, ambiguous and
unmatched shared-path removals, duplicate removals, an unknown file,
and an empty table.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* docs(table): pin Positions iteration-safety semantics

Document that RoaringPositionBitmap.Positions captures the key set up
front while consulting each bucket lazily, so the bitmap must not be
mutated during iteration — consistent with the rest of the type, which
is not safe for concurrent use.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* fix(table): address review feedback on RowDelta DV supersession

Close the converse validation gap: the delta validated that every
removed DV has a replacement among the added delete files, but not
that every added replacement's data file has its live DV removed. A
supersession delta could add a replacement DV for a data file whose
live DV was not in RemoveDeletes, committing two live DVs on that
file — a v3 spec violation that scan planning then rejects. The
manifest walk the removals already perform now also collects every
live DV whose referenced data file gets a replacement in this delta,
and validation requires each to be among the resolved removals.
Deltas without removals do not pay for (or get) this check; plain
AddDeletes stays unvalidated, matching Java, and is called out as
follow-up work. The same pass also rejects two added replacement DVs
referencing one data file — guaranteed corruption regardless of
removals — and detects tables already corrupted with duplicate live
DV entries, both at one Puffin path (where the producer would
tombstone every matching entry while the summary counts one removal)
and across distinct paths (where the sibling duplicate would survive
next to the replacement).

Also from review:

  - a removal-only delta now reaches the replacement-required error
    instead of failing the empty-delta guard with a message that never
    mentions removals,
  - removals require format version >= 3 up front, instead of failing
    resolution with a confusing does-not-belong lookup error on v2,
  - a live Puffin DV entry without a recorded referenced data file
    gets its own error instead of being reported as a non-DV,
  - RemoveDeletes documents that a single live entry at the removed
    path is selected regardless of the caller copy's reference (the
    reference only disambiguates shared paths), and both RemoveDeletes
    and Commit document that removal-carrying commits are
    non-replayable: a CAS conflict fails with ErrCommitFailed and the
    caller must rebuild against a reloaded table,
  - the post-commit validator comment no longer claims the producer is
    always fast-append.

New tests cover the surviving-live-DV rejection, duplicate
replacements for one data file, removal-only deltas, both
duplicate-live-DV corruption shapes, the v2 guard, and an end-to-end
RowDelta supersession race pinning fail-on-first-CAS-conflict with the
peer's DV as the sole survivor.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

fix(table): look up removed-file partition specs by ID (#1816)
body:
accumulateSummaryDelta resolved partition specs two different ways.
Added files went through sp.spec(int(df.SpecID())), a by-ID lookup over
GetSpecByID, while removed data files, delete files and deletion
vectors indexed the spec slice directly with specs[df.SpecID()].

Spec ID is an identifier, not a slice position. RemovePartitionSpecs
filters the slice without renumbering the survivors, and specs loaded
from metadata keep the partition-specs array order, so the two come
apart on ordinary tables. The index expression is evaluated as a call
argument, so it fails before removeFile ever runs: a Delete, Overwrite
or RewriteFiles commit that removes files panics with index out of
range, or silently attributes the change to the wrong partition when
the ID stays in bounds but points at the wrong entry.

Use sp.spec() in the three removal loops so both halves of the function
agree, and drop the now-unused local. Unknown IDs then yield an empty
unpartitioned spec instead of panicking, matching the add path.

The regression test evolves specs 0/1/2, removes spec 1 so the slice
becomes [id0, id2], then sends the same spec-2 data file down both
branches and asserts they report the same changed partition.

Fixes #1815

subject: feat(table): allow added data files to target any registered partition spec (#1818)

* feat(table): allow added data files to target any registered partition spec

The snapshot producer already groups added files by their SpecID and
writes one manifest per spec, but AddDataFiles rejected any DataFile
whose spec id was not the current default, making the producer's
multi-spec add path unreachable. It also resolved each group's spec
through the sp.spec helper, which silently substitutes an empty spec on
lookup failure — a manifest whose declared spec disagrees with its
entries' partition tuples.

Validate each file's partition tuple against its own registered spec —
the shape of Java's MergingSnapshotProducer — error on unregistered
spec ids in both the validation and the producer, and iterate spec
groups in sorted order for deterministic manifest output. This lets
writers keep producing under a previous spec after a partition
evolution and lets rewrites migrate files between specs.

subject: fix(deps): bump twmb/avro to v1.8.0 and adapt to its API changes (#1843)
body:
v1.8.0 changes Schema.Root() to return *SchemaNode rather than SchemaNode,
which breaks four value-context uses here. Field access auto-derefs, so the
fix is a deref at the sites that pass or assign the node by value.

It also changes what integral JSON metadata decodes to. Root() now preserves
numeric precision, so a field's "field-id" property comes back as int64
where it was float64 before (integers above 2^53 previously rounded through
float64). schemaFieldID matched only int and float64, so under v1.8.0 it
returned false for every field.

That failure is silent rather than loud: getFieldIDMap ends up with an empty
map, avroEncodePartitionData iterates nothing, and partition values are
written to the manifest as null. The header schema is still correct, and the
read path drops the same keys for the same reason, so nothing errors --
partition data is just lost. Pinned by the two existing tests that catch it,
TestDataFileStatisticsDecimalPartitionManifestRoundTrip and
TestCollectDeadPositionDeletesPartitioned.

Accepting int64 alongside int and float64 keeps this working across both
avro versions.

subject: fix(partitions,sort): accept ordinal source IDs when decoding (#1665)
body:
* fix(partitions,sort): accept ordinal source IDs when decoding

Decoding rejected source-id 0 in partition specs and sort orders, but
positivity is only an invariant for specs already bound to a schema.
Create-table and commit requests carry unbound specs whose source IDs
are the client's ordinal placeholders: Spark numbers the root struct's
fields from zero, so partitioning or sorting by a table's first column
sends source-id 0. Those requests failed with "source ID must be
positive: 0".

Reject only negative IDs during decoding and leave positivity to schema
binding, which is where Java enforces it. TableMetadata.newTableMetadata
assigns fresh IDs and remaps each spec field by looking the source name
up in the request schema; reassignIDs already does the same, so ordinal
IDs were handled correctly once past decoding. Non-resolvable IDs are
still caught: AddPartitionFieldBySourceID and SortOrder.CheckCompatibility
report source IDs missing from the schema.

Regression tests cover a create-table request numbered from zero through
NewMetadata and a metadata round trip, for both partition specs and sort
orders.

subject: fix(table): drain RollingDataWriter's recordCh on mid-stream write errors (#1851)
body:
* fix(table): drain RollingDataWriter's recordCh on mid-stream write errors

When stream() exits early on a write error, it deregisters itself from
writerFactory.writers before abortAll() can run, so batches already
queued in recordCh were never released.

A lockless drain is not enough: an Add that has passed its closed check
can still enqueue after the drain sees the channel empty, stranding a
retained record. Add and stream's shutdown now share an RWMutex barrier.
Add holds the read lock across its check-and-enqueue; stream's cleanup
cancels the context (releasing any parked send), takes the write lock
(which blocks until every active Add has returned), sets noMoreSends so
later Add calls bail before retaining, then drains. recordCh is never
closed from stream, so a live sender can't hit a closed channel.

Fixes #1825.

Signed-off-by: deepak-2605 <108828387+deepak-2605@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(table): address review — guard cleanup cancel, fix test goroutine leaks

Review follow-up for #1851:

- Only cancel ctx from stream's cleanup on the error exit. The clean
  exit reaches cleanup after closeInput already closed the input with
  all senders finished, so there are no parked sends to release and
  cancelling there only signalled a failure that did not happen. Gated
  behind an exitedCleanly flag.
- Reword the "recordCh is never closed here" comment: another goroutine
  may close it via closeInput, and the drain's !ok case is what ends the
  loop then — it is not dead code.
- Pair both new tests' manually built writers with defer factory.closeAll()
  (stops the iter.Pull counter goroutine) and defer cancel() (the context
  otherwise leaks if the test bails before stream starts).

subject: fix(updates): decode add-spec and add-sort-order unbound (#1873)
body:
* fix(updates): decode add-spec and add-sort-order unbound

A commit request's add-spec and add-sort-order payloads are bound to a
schema by Apply, not by the decoder: AddPartitionSpec calls BindToSchema
and AddSortOrder calls CheckCompatibility, both against the table's
current schema. Decoding them into the bound types therefore enforced an
invariant the wire form does not carry.

That rejected a spec a client is entitled to send. A dropped partition
field is a void transform over source ID 0, which BindToSchema preserves
as a tombstone, so re-sending a spec after dropping a partition column
failed with "partition source ID must be positive: 0" before binding ran.

Decode into UnboundPartitionSpec and UnboundSortOrder, and hand the
embedded bound values to the builder. Source IDs that do not resolve are
still rejected, now by binding, which reports them against the schema
that decides. The constructors keep taking bound values, so callers are
unaffected, and Apply reports a nil payload rather than dereferencing it.

* fix(updates): exercise the add-spec and add-sort-order assertions

TestUnmarshalUpdates cast both sides of every comparison from the decoded
slice, so each update was compared against itself and the add-spec and
add-sort-order assertions passed vacuously. The add-spec branch was also
labelled "add-partition-spec", which no action matches, so it fell
through to the default branch and never ran at all.

Iterate over the expected updates, switch on the action constants, and
compare the expected value against the decoded one. The sort order
fixture disagreed with its JSON on the null order of the second field,
which the self-comparison hid; the JSON is the source of truth, so the
fixture now says nulls-last.

Assert the binding error the unresolvable source ID test expects, rather
than only the absence of the old decode error, and align the nil payload
guards with the "update %q requires field %q" template that
validateRequiredUpdateFields uses, so both paths read alike.

The addSortOrderUpdate comment claimed a parity with the partition spec
that does not hold. CheckCompatibility still requires every sort source
ID to resolve against the current schema, so decoding unbound defers the
error rather than accepting the field; say that instead.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Pütz <tobias@minio.io>

* docs(partitions,sort): cover the commit path in the unbound types

The unbound spec and sort order types documented themselves as the
create-table request's decode target and told readers to use the bound
types for anything read from table metadata. An add-spec or
add-sort-order commit payload is neither: its source IDs are the current
schema's field IDs, but nothing resolves them until the update is
applied, so decoding it bound enforces an invariant the wire form does
not carry. The types were already right for that payload; only their
docs excluded it.

Describe both wire forms, keep the create-table binding caveat scoped to
the form it applies to, and say that decoding unbound defers the check
rather than dropping it. Note as well that a bound spec's source IDs are
positive apart from the void tombstone a dropped field leaves behind,
which is the one case the bound decoder already lets through.

Also address the review's smaller points: comment that the builder
aliases the update's embedded sort order, because AddSortOrder writes the
fresh order ID into it and keeps a pointer to that field; use
require.ErrorContains where a test pins BindToSchema's wording, so a
regression stops with a useful message; and add the missing happy-path
round trip for the add-sort-order decode, which until now was only
covered on the reject path.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Pütz <tobias@minio.io>

subject: test(table): fix TruncateUpperBoundBinary guard for negative width (#1980)
body:
The negative-width test case ("negative width keeps bound") was added in
#1934 while the stricter truncation-invariant guard was added in #1928.
Each PR was green on its own base, but the rebase-merge combined them:
the guard `tt.truncate < len(tt.value)` matches a negative width (-1 < 2),
so the negative case (where the bound is kept, not truncated) wrongly
falls into the truncation asserts and fails deterministically:

    utils_test.go:128: "2" is not less than or equal to "-1"
    utils_test.go:129: "0" is not greater than "0"

Only assert the shrink/increment invariants when a truncation actually
happened by additionally requiring a non-negative width. The production
TruncateUpperBoundBinary already handles negative widths correctly.

subject: perf(rest): lazy-decode snapshots in commitTableResponse when snapshot-loading-mode=refs (#1956)
body:
* perf(rest): defer unreferenced commit snapshots

Parse REST commit-response metadata without materializing unreferenced snapshot history when snapshot-loading-mode=refs. Validate and index the raw snapshot array synchronously, eagerly decode every branch and tag target, and decode individual historical snapshots by ID on demand.

Materialize the full history only for collection-wide operations such as Snapshots, serialization, equality, builders, and format upgrades. Keep the deferred state pointer-owned and concurrency-safe.

Add correctness, round-trip, validation, and race coverage plus byte-sized benchmarks for eager parsing, referenced access, individual historical lookup, and full materialization.

subject: fix(catalog/sql): return ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists on a concurrent create (#1635)
body:
* fix(catalog/sql): return ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists on a concurrent create

CreateNamespace resolves the namespace key, returns ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists if
it is there, and otherwise inserts. Two callers creating the same namespace both
pass that check, and the loser's insert then violates the primary key on
iceberg_namespace_properties. The driver's error is returned as-is:

  error inserting namespace properties for namespace '[raw]': constraint failed:
  UNIQUE constraint failed: iceberg_namespace_properties.catalog_name, ...

so callers matching errors.Is(err, catalog.ErrNamespaceAlreadyExists) -- the
contract every other catalog implementation honours -- see a create-if-absent
fail for a namespace that does exist.

Re-resolve the key when the insert fails and return the sentinel if the
namespace is now present. An insert that failed for any other reason is
unchanged.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* test(catalog/sql): pin the insert-recovery branch

TestCreateNamespaceConcurrent cannot tell the two paths apart: the check at
1246 and the recovery at 1276 return the same sentinel with the same
formatting, so the counts hold whichever one a goroutine took.

Adds a test that only passes if the insert ran and failed. A driver wrapper
plants the row on the same connection just before the catalog's insert, as its
own statement -- sqlite rolls back the failing statement's own changes,
including anything a trigger did, so the plant has to be separate.

The re-check now runs in the transaction. On a separate connection it could not
see an uncommitted winner, and with a constrained pool it deadlocked waiting
for a connection the open transaction was holding.

Also collects unexpected errors in the concurrent test and asserts after the
drain, so one stray error does not report as three failures.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/sql): recover the create race with a savepoint

The insert-failure recovery re-queried the namespace on the same tx. On
Postgres a failed statement aborts the whole transaction (25P02), so that
re-check came back an error rather than a row and the raw duplicate-key
error was returned -- the pre-PR behaviour. The fix was inert on Postgres,
one of the five declared dialects, and SQLite masked it by rolling back
only the failing statement.

Wrap the insert in a savepoint (bun's nested transaction, which emits the
right syntax per dialect, including MSSQL's SAVE TRANSACTION). On failure,
roll back to the savepoint so the transaction is usable again, then
re-check. The race-loser now returns the sentinel in the same form as the
serial pre-check so the two paths are identical; the rollback- and
re-check-failure branches join their causes instead of dropping them.

TestCreateNamespaceLosesInsertRace drives a driver that emulates the
Postgres abort -- refusing statements after the failed insert until a
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT -- so it fails without the savepoint and passes with
it, which the previous SQLite-only planting driver could not show. Adds a
negative test that an unrelated insert failure surfaces its own error, and
a note that the driver name depends on databaseName() being unique.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/sql): gate the create-race savepoint to Postgres

Oracle has no RELEASE SAVEPOINT, so sp.Commit() on the happy path would
fail and roll back a good insert. Only Postgres aborts the whole tx on a
failed statement, so only it needs the savepoint to keep the re-check
runnable; other dialects take a plain insert + re-check.

The emulated-Postgres recovery tests now build the catalog with the
Postgres dialect and assert the insert interceptor actually fired.

* test(catalog/sql): pin non-Postgres recovery and savepoint happy path

Add a deterministic SQLite-dialect test (non-aborting dupInsertDriver) for
the non-Postgres recovery branch, and an insertSucceeds mode covering the
Postgres SAVEPOINT -> insert -> RELEASE happy path. Both previously ran at
coverage count 0. Also scope the gate comment to the dialects reasoned about.

* test(catalog/sql): assert the savepoint happy path persists the row

The success-path test only checked the nil return, so swapping RELEASE
SAVEPOINT for ROLLBACK left it green while zero rows persisted. Let the
insertSucceeds probe read real persistence and assert the namespace
survives the commit, so a rolled-back savepoint fails the test.

subject: fix(table): convert int-backed decimal row group bounds (#2009)
body:
Parquet plain-encodes INT32/INT64-backed decimal statistics little-endian,
while an Iceberg bound is big-endian two's complement. TestRowGroup stored
the stat bytes as bounds unchanged, so they decoded to unrelated values and
pruned row groups that do match, silently dropping rows from scan results.

Reverse the stat bytes for those two physical types before storing them,
in a parquetStatsBounds helper that any evaluator populating bounds from
Parquet statistics should go through. FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY-backed decimals
are already big-endian in Parquet and pass through untouched. The reversed
4- or 8-byte bounds are wider than the spec's minimum width, but they are
only used in memory and UnmarshalBinary is width-tolerant, so they decode
as-is. arrow-go plain-encodes little-endian on big-endian hosts too, so the
conversion does not depend on the host architecture.

Closes #1876

subject: feat(table): add tunables to bound compaction pipeline memory (#1993)
body:
* Add tunables bounding compaction pipeline memory

The compaction read+write pipeline had fixed memory characteristics:
the scanner decodes read.parquet.batch-size rows per Arrow batch
(131072 by default) with no per-scan override, and each rolling data
writer buffers up to 64 record batches in its input channel with no way
to lower or raise that bound. On wide rows the product of those two
numbers dominates a compaction worker's peak memory.

- WithArrowBatchSize scan option caps the rows decoded per Arrow batch
  for one scan, overriding the table's read.parquet.batch-size without
  mutating caller-supplied scan options.
- The rolling data writers' record channel capacity (default 64
  batches) is now configurable via the WithRecordBatchBufferSize write
  option, threaded through recordWritingArgs to the writer factory. It
  applies to both the fanout and the clustered write paths, which share
  the rolling writer.
- WithParquetRowGroupLimit write option overrides the table's
  write.parquet.row-group-limit per write, bounding rows buffered per
  row group before each flush.
- Compaction group options forward all three into
  ExecuteCompactionGroup: WithCompactionReadBatchSize,
  WithCompactionRecordBatchBufferSize, and
  WithCompactionParquetRowGroupLimit.

subject: perf(table): bound the scan reorder heap at scan concurrency above one (#2039)
body:
* perf(table): add lagging-task reorder heap benchmark and test

BenchmarkArrowScanReorderHeapLaggingTask in
table/arrow_scanner_reorder_bench_test.go scans M single-batch data
files at WithMaxConcurrency(4) with the Open of task 0's file gated
until the other M - 1 files have been read, and reports the peak
HeapInuse delta while the gate is closed and the number of batches the
other files produced in that window. On Apple M3 Pro, 11 cores,
go1.25.9, -count=3, the delta is 4.7 MB at M = 8, 20 to 23 MB at
M = 32 and 96 MB at M = 128, with M - 1 batches held every time.

TestArrowScanReorderHeapBoundedWhileHeadTaskLags in
table/arrow_scanner_reorder_test.go runs the same scan inside a
testing/synctest bubble. synctest.Wait returns once every scan
goroutine is durably blocked, so the count of out-of-order batches the
pipeline holds is read at a fixed point with no sleeps, both before a
fix (all M - 1 other files are read) and after one (workers park on
credits). It asserts the count never exceeds numWorkers x K with K = 2
as reorderCreditsPerWorker. On main it fails with 31 held batches
against a bound of 8, then releases the gate, checks that every row
arrives and checks that the CheckedAllocator is empty.

Refs #2038.

Signed-off-by: KranzL <50032317+KranzL@users.noreply.github.com>

* perf(table): bound the scan reorder heap at scan concurrency above one

Each scan worker in recordBatchesFromTasksAndDeletes and in
makePositionDeleteRecordsForFilter now holds a task credit. The worker
takes the credit before it takes a task, the credit rides on the
task's Last record, and it comes back when the iterator's consumer
takes that record, when the deferred drain loop takes it, or when
MakeSequencedChanWithDiscard discards it at close. A worker waiting
for its credit also waits on the scan context, so cancellation still
stops it. Error records carry no credit.

A worker therefore cannot start its next task while any batch of its
previous task is still in the records channel, the reorder heap or
the sequenced channel. While the head task lags, each other worker
finishes one task and parks, so the heap holds at most numWorkers - 1
tasks instead of every task the free workers can reach. Decoding
inside a task is not throttled and the head task's worker never waits.

Per-batch credits, as #2038 proposed, were measured first on
BenchmarkArrowScanManyFilesAndBatches (32 files of 32 one-row batches,
concurrency 4): K = 2 took 141.6 ms/op against 69.4 ms/op on main,
K = 8 took 127.9 ms/op and K = 32 took 78.7 ms/op, because the batches
a free worker may run ahead are the scan's parallelism. With the
per-task credit that benchmark is within noise of main in interleaved
runs (benchstat, n = 10: +0.4%, -0.2% and +1.5% on the three
sub-benchmarks), and BenchmarkArrowScanReorderHeapLaggingTask holds 3
gated batches and 2.0 to 2.3 MB of peak heap delta for M = 8, 32 and
128, where main holds M - 1 batches and 4.7, 20 to 25 and 95 MB.

The doc on WithCompactionArrowBatchSize now states the bound that
holds, workers x (rows in the largest task + n) +
(recordBatchBufferSize + 2) x n rows, and WithCompactionScanConcurrency
says its worker count multiplies the read-side term.

TestArrowScanReorderHeapBoundedWhileHeadTaskLags asserts the bound of
(numWorkers - 1) x maxInFlightTasksPerWorker completed out-of-order
tasks. TestArrowScanReorderCancelWhileWorkersWaitForTaskCredits
cancels the scan while the free workers are parked and checks that the
iterator returns context.Canceled, every scan goroutine exits and every
batch is released.

Fixes #2038.

Signed-off-by: KranzL <50032317+KranzL@users.noreply.github.com>

* perf(table): hand the scan credit to exactly one record and test the compaction bound

recordSink now tracks whether its worker holds a credit and hands it to
exactly one record: the task's Last record in send, or the error record
in fail when no Last record was sent. processRecords can send Last and
then return an error from the reader or the deferred close, so fail
hands off nil in that case. No path abandons a credit any more, and a
worker that failed and went back to reserve would wait only until its
error record leaves the sequenced channel. The three delete-loader
error sites in recordBatchesFromTasksAndDeletes go through sink.fail,
so fail is the only path that puts an error record into records.
recordSink is a pointer built only by newRecordSink, so a nil sink
panics on first use instead of hanging on a nil channel send. The nil
guard in acquire is gone; taskCredits is declared before
enumeratedRecord.

Scan.ReadTasks now states the bound for the general scan: each worker
holds the decoded batches of at most one task until the iterator has
returned them, so the batches waiting behind a slow early task total at
most the worker count times the rows in the largest task, rounded up to
a multiple of the batch size, and one large file among small ones still
holds its whole decoded contents while it waits. ToArrowRecords and
WithMaxConcurrency point at that paragraph.

TestRecordSinkHandsOffCreditOnce covers fail without Last, Last followed
by fail, and that reserve blocks while the credit is out.
TestExecuteCompactionGroupRecordPipelineBounded drives
ExecuteCompactionGroup with four scan workers and a writer queue of two
over 32 single-batch files inside testing/synctest, gating task 0 in
Open and then the output file in Create, and checks 3 fully read tasks
while task 0 is gated and exactly 8 while the writer is gated, the two
terms of the bound on WithCompactionArrowBatchSize counted in tasks.
With the credit gate disabled the counts are 31 and 32.

Signed-off-by: KranzL <50032317+KranzL@users.noreply.github.com>

* test(table): write uncompressed parquet in the synctest compaction fixture

TestExecuteCompactionGroupRecordPipelineBounded wrote zstd parquet
inside its synctest bubble. arrow-go keeps zstd encoders in a global
sync.Pool and klauspost's Encoder creates its encoders channel on first
use, so the first zstd write inside the bubble left a pooled encoder
whose channel belongs to the bubble. When a later test reused that
encoder, go1.25.9 failed the whole package with "receive on synctest
channel from outside bubble" (seen in TestClusteredWriter on the
ubuntu and macos go1.25.9 jobs; go1.26.1 passes). Locally the pool was
usually cleared by GC before the next zstd write, which is why the
suite passed here; with GOGC=off it fails every time.

The reorder fixture now sets write.parquet.compression-codec to
uncompressed, so no codec pool is touched inside the bubble. With
GOGC=off the pair TestExecuteCompactionGroupRecordPipelineBounded and
TestClusteredWriter passes three times in a row.

Signed-off-by: KranzL <50032317+KranzL@users.noreply.github.com>

body:
* feat(schema): add AssignFreshSchemaIDsWithBase

Port Java's TypeUtil.assignFreshIds(schema, baseSchema, nextId). Fields
whose full column name exists in the base schema reuse its ID; all
others get fresh IDs from nextID. This lets callers evolve a table
schema declaratively without reusing retired column IDs, by passing the
current schema as base and counting up from last-column-id.

AssignFreshSchemaIDs now delegates to the new function with a nil base.

* fix(schema): return errors instead of panicking in AssignFreshSchemaIDsWithBase

  IDs can't collide with IDs reused from base.
- Check for duplicate field IDs before building the schema, so a nextID
  that returns IDs that are too low gives an error instead of a panic.
- Return an error for identifier field IDs that aren't in the schema,
  instead of mapping them to 0.
- Document the nextID range and case-sensitive name matching.
- Rename setFreshIDs.visiting to source.
- Add tests for list<struct>, the nil nextID path, and new and stale
  identifier fields.

* fix(schema): assign sibling field IDs before recursing

Java's AssignFreshIds.struct gives IDs to all fields of a struct before
visiting their nested types. We handed out IDs depth-first, so nested
schemas got different IDs than Java (and Rust, per the old TODOs in
TestReassignIds) would give them.

This changes the IDs AssignFreshSchemaIDs gives new tables with nested
columns, so the table fixtures that hardcoded the old order are updated.

subject: fix(table/dv): read deletion vectors by content_offset when the file is not a Puffin container (#2071)
body:
* fix(table/dv): read deletion vectors by content_offset when the file is not a Puffin container

Databricks writes deletion vectors for IcebergCompatV3 (UniForm) tables as a
Delta deletion_vector_*.bin file: a one-byte version prefix followed by
deletion-vector-v1 blobs, with no Puffin header or footer. The manifest entry
is well-formed (file_format=PUFFIN, referenced_data_file, content_offset,
content_size_in_bytes point at a valid blob), and the Java reference reader
(BaseDeleteLoader.readDV) reads such files because it never consults the
Puffin footer: it reads content_size_in_bytes bytes at content_offset.

ReadDV/ReadDVs opened the file with puffin.NewReader first and failed with
"puffin: invalid header magic" on these tables.

- puffin: NewReader wraps the header-magic and too-small errors in a new
  sentinel, ErrNotPuffinFile, so callers can detect "no Puffin container".
- table/dv: when the DV file is not a Puffin container, fall back to reading
  the blobs directly at content_offset (Java parity). The blob's length,
  magic and CRC-32 are still verified by DeserializeDV and the decoded
  cardinality is validated against the manifest record_count; footer-only
  checks (blob type, referenced-data-file property, cardinality property)
  are skipped with a slog warning. Real Puffin files keep the existing
  strict path unchanged.

Verified against a Databricks Unity Catalog IcebergCompatV3 table read through
the UC Iceberg REST catalog with vended credentials: 968,980 rows after
1,020 deletes + 1,020 updates, matching the SQL result; copy-on-write and
non-DV tables unaffected.

Fixes #2070

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01MqCR5xLuYcb7Baw6Xbj4be

* fix(table/dv): scope ErrNotPuffinFile to magic-first, reuse the open handle for bare DV reads

Review follow-up:

- puffin.NewReader checks the header magic before the minimum-size guard.
  ErrNotPuffinFile is returned only when the file is too short to hold the
  magic or the leading bytes are not PFA1; a file that starts with the magic
  but is truncated keeps the plain "puffin: file too small" error, so a
  partial upload of a real Puffin file is never routed to the bare-blob path.
- openDVReader returns the still-open file (nil reader) on ErrNotPuffinFile;
  readBareDVs reads from that handle instead of reopening the path.
- readBareDVs no longer re-runs validateDVFile (both callers validate before
  dispatch; documented), reads blobs in content_offset order and restores
  input order, and logs the "not a Puffin container" warning once per file
  path, after the first blob decoded.
- Tests: truncated / corrupt-footer Puffin files fail without wrapping
  ErrNotPuffinFile; bare blob with corrupt CRC surfaces the "blob at offset"
  wrap; reversed-offset input keeps output order; puffin size test uses a
  valid-magic short file plus a too-short-for-magic case.

Re-verified against a fresh Databricks IcebergCompatV3 table with two
deletion vectors: 999,000 rows / 1,000 updated markers, matching SQL.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01MqCR5xLuYcb7Baw6Xbj4be

subject: fix(catalog/rest): sign SigV4 with credentials from catalog properties (#1999)
body:
* fix(catalog/rest): sign SigV4 with credentials from catalog properties

The REST catalog's SigV4 signer only used the AWS default credential chain
(config.LoadDefaultConfig), ignoring the s3.* credential properties passed to
the catalog. This forced callers targeting AWS SigV4 REST catalogs (S3 Tables,
Glue) to export AWS_* environment variables even when they supplied credentials
via catalog properties.

Build a static credentials provider from s3.access-key-id / s3.secret-access-key
/ s3.session-token when present, and only fall back to the default chain
otherwise. An explicitly provided aws.Config (WithAwsConfig) still wins.

This mirrors the same gap tracked for the Python client in
apache/iceberg-python#2070.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* test(catalog/rest): pin SigV4 props-cred signing; error on partial creds

Address review feedback:
- Add TestSigV4SignsWithPropsCredentials, which asserts the SigV4 Authorization
  header is signed with the credentials from catalog properties. This pins the
  wiring: removing the cfg.Credentials assignment makes the test fail.
- staticCredsFromProps now returns an error when only one of the access-key /
  secret-access-key pair is set, instead of silently falling back to the ambient
  default identity. Neither set still falls back to the default chain.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* docs(catalog/rest): document SigV4 signing credential precedence

Address review feedback (minor): the SigV4 signing identity resolves as
WithAwsConfig > s3.* catalog properties > AWS default credential chain. Document
this on WithSigV4 and in the rest.sigv4-enabled configuration reference.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/rest): error on incomplete SigV4 creds via ValidateStaticCredentials

Delegate staticCredsFromProps to internal/awsconfig.ValidateStaticCredentials so
a token-only s3.session-token (no access/secret key) returns the
ErrIncompleteStaticCredentials sentinel instead of silently dropping to the
default credential chain. Add a token-only test case and assert the sentinel via
errors.Is. Document the s3.* vs Java rest.* divergence in the WithSigV4 godoc and
configuration.md.

* feat(catalog/rest): accept Java rest.* SigV4 credential aliases

Accept rest.access-key-id / rest.secret-access-key / rest.session-token as
aliases for the s3.* signing-credential properties, resolved per field with the
s3.* keys taking precedence. This lets operators migrating from the Java client
configure SigV4 signing with the property names they already use instead of
silently falling through to the AWS default credential chain.

* fix(catalog/rest): harden SigV4 credential boundaries

Two credential-boundary fixes for the props-based SigV4 signing path:

- Resolve the credential tuple atomically per namespace. Resolving each field
  independently let a partial s3.* pair be completed with a rest.* field (or
  inherit an unrelated rest.* token), signing as a hybrid identity that still
  passed validation. Now if any s3.* field is set we validate and use only the
  s3.* tuple, otherwise only the rest.* tuple; never backfill across namespaces.

- Do not re-sign a cross-origin redirect. sessionTransport signed every hop, so
  a redirect to a different origin exposed the SigV4 Authorization header and
  session token to an unconfigured host. Signing is now skipped when the request
  origin (scheme/host/effective port) differs from the configured catalog origin.

Tests cover the mixed-partial and s3-pair-plus-rest-token cases and assert a
cross-origin redirect target receives neither the Authorization header nor the
session token. Also closes a response body left open in an existing test.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

subject: fix(catalog/sql): widen the write-retry budget for lock contention (#2036)
body:
* fix(catalog/sql): widen the write-retry budget for lock contention

Concurrent CreateTable/CreateView against a SQLite catalog could fail with
SQLITE_BUSY instead of ErrTableAlreadyExists/ErrViewAlreadyExists.

SQLite serializes writers, and the write transaction in these paths reads
(namespace existence, identifier availability) before it inserts. A lock
conflict on that upgrade is reported immediately and does not consult the busy
handler, so a busy timeout cannot absorb it -- only retrying the whole
transaction can, which retrySerializableWriteTx already does. The budget was
just too small: 3 attempts with 10ms/20ms backoff is 30ms of waiting, and a
loaded machine holds the write lock longer than that. When the budget ran out
before the winning transaction committed, the losing caller saw the driver's
lock error rather than the catalog conflict it should report.

Raise the budget to 6 attempts (~310ms). It costs nothing without contention,
since the delays only apply between failed attempts.

This was observed as a flaky TestConcurrentTableViewCollisionReturnsCatalogSentinel,
which failed on main and on unrelated pull requests.

The new regression test makes the contention deterministic by holding the
database write lock for longer than the old budget; it fails before this change
and passes after.

Signed-off-by: Matt Topol <zotthewizard@gmail.com>

* fix(catalog/sql): tighten contention test margin, document cross-dialect budget

fails with "no default path set".

Detect the federated database and create such tables in two phases,
mirroring pyiceberg: create a minimal Glue entry so S3 Tables allocates
storage, read the assigned location, write Iceberg metadata to it, then
repoint the Glue entry. The allocated entry is rolled back on any later
failure. An explicit location is rejected for these tables, and a missing
version id is treated as a failed commit.

S3 Tables entries also report a service-specific Glue TableType (e.g.
"customer"), so getRawTable now accepts any entry marked as Iceberg via
the table_type parameter, not only EXTERNAL_TABLE.

Adds unit coverage for detection, the two-phase create, location
rejection, every rollback path, and the relaxed TableType gate, plus a
gated live integration test.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/glue): don't roll back S3 Tables table on reload failure

The final LoadTable ran inside the create's rollback scope, so a
transient read failure after a successful commit deleted an
already-created table (and reclaimed its storage). Move the reload out
of that scope: only allocate/write/commit failures roll back now, which
also matches the generic create path. Document that S3 Tables keeps its
own Glue TableType on the commit update.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* test(catalog/glue): reload a service TableType in the S3 Tables create test

Have the successful create path's mocked reload return a service-specific
TableType ("customer"), so the happy path also exercises the relaxed
getRawTable gate rather than only EXTERNAL_TABLE.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* address review: lazy federation detection and scope getRawTable relaxation

- CreateTable now tries the generic path first and only probes for S3 Tables
  federation when location resolution fails with ErrNoDefaultLocation. This
  removes the redundant GetDatabase on default creates and avoids a new
  glue:GetDatabase requirement on explicit-location creates.
- Export internal.ErrNoDefaultLocation so the probe matches it via errors.Is
  instead of the error string.
- Scope the relaxed getRawTable TableType gate to entries actually federated
  to S3 Tables (Table.FederatedTable.ConnectionType == aws:s3tables), so
  non-federated databases keep their pre-existing behavior.
- Tests: prove explicit-location creates skip the probe, prove a non-federated
  iceberg-param table is still rejected, and update federated mocks.

* address review: reject explicit S3 Tables location, soften federation probe

- CreateTable rejects an explicit location for a federated S3 Tables
  database instead of silently creating a table outside managed storage.
- isS3TablesDatabase treats AccessDeniedException as not-federated so a
  caller lacking glue:GetDatabase still reaches the generic create path.
- Document the two residual create failures left to the service.
- Tighten the metadata-write-failure test to assert the write error.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* catalog/glue: best-effort clean up S3 Tables metadata on commit failure

When UpdateTable fails after WriteMetadata, the rollback now best-effort
deletes the written metadata object before dropping the minimal Glue entry.
For S3 Tables the managed location may be unreachable, so the removal error
is ignored and reclaiming any remainder is left to the service, as documented.
The existing UpdateTable-failure test now asserts the metadata file is gone.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* catalog/glue: make stranded S3 Tables entry droppable and harden the commit

- DropTable/getRawTable now accept a minimal federated S3 Tables entry
  (format=ICEBERG, no table_type), so a double-failure leftover is cleaned
  up through DropTable, restoring parity with pyiceberg's delete_table.
- The UpdateTable repoint preserves the service-assigned TableType instead
  of forcing EXTERNAL_TABLE, which S3 Tables rejects on write; a unit test
  now asserts the TableType we send.
- The rollback DeleteTable runs on a context detached from a cancelled
  create (context.WithoutCancel + timeout) and joins errors with errors.Join.
- isS3TablesDatabase guards against a nil Database from getDatabase.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* catalog/glue: keep the live-proven EXTERNAL_TABLE on the S3 Tables repoint

Sending the allocated entry's own TableType was untested against S3 Tables
and races the service's federation (nil right after CreateTable, "customer"
once federated). Live testing confirmed S3 Tables accepts EXTERNAL_TABLE on
the repoint, so send it unconditionally and assert it in the unit test.

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* catalog/glue: note S3 Tables ignores the repoint TableType (verified live)

Signed-off-by: iremcaginyurtturk <cagin.yurtturk@getbruin.com>

* fix(catalog/glue): write table metadata with the catalog AWS config

The metadata writes in CreateTable, commitS3TablesTable, and CommitTable used
a bare context, so the S3 FileIO resolver fell back to LoadDefaultConfig. A
catalog built with WithAwsConfig or glue.* static credentials would then call
Glue as the configured principal but PUT metadata as the ambient one (or fail
despite valid configured credentials). Wrap the context with the catalog's AWS
config before each write, matching RegisterTable and convertGlueToIceberg; for
commitS3TablesTable this also covers the staged.FS metadata cleanup.

* test(catalog/glue): mock GetDatabase in TestGlueCreateTableAlreadyExists

Merging main brought in TestGlueCreateTableAlreadyExists, which does an
explicit-location create. CreateTable now consults the database up front to
reject federated S3 Tables locations, so the test must mock GetDatabase; a
non-federated result lets it take the generic path and assert the
AlreadyExists mapping. In real AWS a missing glue:GetDatabase surfaces as
AccessDenied, which isS3TablesDatabase already treats as non-federated.

- CreateTable now fetches the database once and decides S3 Tables federation for

  properties so staging issues no second GetDatabase. This also catches catalogs
  with a `warehouse` property, where the previous lazy probe let a federated
  create write outside the managed storage.

- Reject RenameTable for federated S3 Tables tables, whose managed storage the
  copy-then-delete rename cannot safely repoint.
- Replace isS3TablesDatabase with lookupDatabase (AccessDenied/NotFound tolerant)

rejection; catalog-id pinning; and AssertExpectations on the fall-through test.

body:
* refactor(table)!: extract orphan cleanup into table/maintenance

This is Slice 1 of issue #2083, breaking pre-v1 relocation of the orphan cleanup
service from the table package into a dedicated table/maintenance package.

Changes:
- Create new table/maintenance package with Service facade
- Move DeleteOrphanFiles, PlanOrphanFiles, ExecuteOrphanCleanup, and PurgeFiles
  methods from table.Table to maintenance.Service
- Move exported types: OrphanCleanupOption, OrphanCleanupResult, OrphanCleanupPlan,
  OrphanFile, PrefixMismatchMode (and constants)
- Move helper functions: WithLocation, WithFilesOlderThan, WithDryRun,
  WithDeleteFunc, WithCleanupMaxConcurrency, WithPrefixMismatchMode,
  WithEqualSchemes, WithEqualAuthorities
- Export IsGCEnabled from table package (was unexported isGCEnabled)
- Update all callers in catalog/ and cmd/iceberg/ to use new API:
  maintenance.New(tbl).DeleteOrphanFiles(...) instead of tbl.DeleteOrphanFiles(...)
- Move tests to table/maintenance package
- Update IsGCEnabled references in transaction.go and updates.go

The new public entry shape maintains ergonomic parity with the original API.
To use orphan cleanup: create a maintenance service with maintenance.New(table),
then call its methods.

BREAKING: table.DeleteOrphanFiles, table.PlanOrphanFiles, table.ExecuteOrphanCleanup,
and table.PurgeFiles are no longer available on table.Table. Use table/maintenance
package instead.

* style(table): gofmt the moved orphan-cleanup test

table/maintenance/orphan_cleanup_test.go was not gofmt-clean after the move (a
block comment needed re-indentation), which failed the golangci-lint gofmt check
in CI. Formatting only, no behavior change.

* refactor(table/maintenance): use free functions and restore dropped tests

Address review feedback on the orphan-cleanup extraction:

- Replace the Service facade with free functions that take the table as their
  first argument (maintenance.DeleteOrphanFiles(ctx, tbl, ...)), matching
  table/compaction, and update all callers in catalog/ and cmd/iceberg/. This
  avoids freezing a stateful constructor at v1; a deprecation shim on
  table.Table is impossible anyway because table/maintenance imports table.
- Rename the four generic options to the WithCleanup* prefix
  (WithCleanupLocation/DryRun/DeleteFunc/FilesOlderThan) for consistency with
  WithCleanupMaxConcurrency before the names freeze.
- Restore the tests and benchmarks dropped in the move: the statistics- and
  tombstone-reference tests, the manifest-dedup and concurrency-limit tests,
  the negative-/zero-age retention checks, and the PurgeFiles and manifest-list
  benchmarks, porting their shared IO and manifest helpers into the package.
- Document table.IsGCEnabled's parsing rules now that it is exported, and add a
  package doc comment.
- Fix website/src/api.md and releases.md (with a moved-symbols compatibility
  note), and add a `make vet` target running `go vet -tags=integration ./...`
  (wired into CI) so the moved //go:build integration test stays compiled.

* docs(table/maintenance): document OrphanCleanupOption and the WithCleanup* options

Add one-line doc comments with defaults to OrphanCleanupOption,
WithCleanupLocation (table data location), WithCleanupFilesOlderThan (72h),
and WithCleanupDryRun (false), now that the WithCleanup* names are fixed for v1.

subject: fix(catalog/rest): don't bind the cached vended-credential FileIO to the caller's context (#2079)
body:
* fix(catalog/rest): don't bind the cached vended-credential FileIO to the caller's context

vendedCredentialRefresher.loadFS caches the FileIO it builds and hands it
to every later caller, but built it with the first caller's ctx. The GCS
filesystem keeps the context it is opened with, so once that ctx was
cancelled every later operation through the table failed with
context.Canceled, even when called with a live context. Any writer that
scopes each commit to its own context (e.g. context.WithTimeout) saw
every commit after the first fail. Renewal had the same issue, and so
did prefixScopedIO, which stores the ctx and opens filesystems lazily.

Build the cached IO from context.WithoutCancel(ctx): values are kept,
cancellation is not. fetchCreds still honours ctx.

Fixes #2078

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stephane Loeuillet <stephane.loeuillet@kaiko.com>

* fix(catalog/rest): let the refresher own the vended FileIO's lifetime

Review follow-up. Detaching the cached IO from the caller's cancellation
left close() as the only teardown, and renewal replaced the cached IO
without closing it, so a superseded IO's background work leaked.

The refresher now opens the IO on its own cancellable context, derived
from context.WithoutCancel(ctx). Renewal installs the new IO, then closes
the superseded one and cancels its context; a failed renewal cancels only
the context it created and keeps the cached IO. close() closes the IO and
cancels its context.

newPrefixScopedIO keeps the context it is given (documented): that is how
close reaches the filesystems it opens lazily.

Tests: renewal is asserted to rebuild the IO on a distinct context, keep
values, and retire the old IO; close and a failed renewal are covered;
first-caller value inheritance is documented rather than promised; checked
type assertion.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stephane Loeuillet <stephane.loeuillet@kaiko.com>

* fix(catalog/rest): keep the superseded vended FileIO usable on renewal

Review follow-up. Closing and cancelling the superseded IO on renewal
broke callers still holding it (manifest planning batches, partial
rewrites, concurrent scans and writes on derived tables), and the leak it
guarded against does not exist for the gocloud backends. replaceIO is
swap-only again; close() still closes the current IO and cancels its
context.

Tests now run on a real blobfs.FileIO over memblob, opened on the
context it is given: the cached IO is used after the first caller's
cancellation, and the IO from before a renewal is used after it (this
fails with "blob: Bucket has been closed" on the previous commit). The
NotSame check, which tested the context's implementation rather than the
renewal, is gone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stephane Loeuillet <stephane.loeuillet@kaiko.com>

* fix(catalog/rest): document why the vended IO keeps ctx values; drop unused test field

Review nits: the S3 factory reads its base AWS config from the context values WithoutCancel keeps, so say so next to it; contextCapturingScheme.scheme was never read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Stephane Loeuillet <stephane.loeuillet@kaiko.com>

* docs(catalog/rest): say why replaceIO drops the superseded cancel

Review nit: calling it would end the context that callers still holding the old IO run on.

subject: ci: add apidiff check for incompatible API changes (#2166)
body:
Part of the v1.0 freeze work in #2062. After the 1.0.0 tag, any breaking
change to the exported API needs a /v2 module, so we want CI to catch them.

The new "API compatibility" workflow runs golang.org/x/exp/cmd/apidiff in
module mode on every pull request. It exports the API of the base branch
tip the PR merges onto and compares the merged result against it. Internal
packages are skipped. The list of incompatible changes goes to the job
summary.

Until 1.0 we still make intentional breaks, so a break only fails the check
when the PR title does not declare it with the Conventional Commits "!"
marker (for example "refactor(io)!: ..."), which the repo already uses for
breaking changes. Editing the title re-runs the check. After the tag, the
title escape hatch can be dropped so any break fails.

If apidiff itself fails, for example because the base or the PR does not
build, the script prints the error and exits 2, so a broken build is not
reported as an API break.

The logic lives in dev/check-api-compat.sh so it can also be run locally
against any base ref. CONTRIBUTING.md now mentions the check and the "!"
convention.

Signed-off-by: laskoviymishka <laskoviymishka@gmail.com>

body:
refactor!: remove deprecated ManifestFile.FetchEntries and DataFile.DistinctValueCounts

ManifestFile.FetchEntries loaded every entry into memory and took no
context. Use ManifestFile.Entries, which streams entries as an iterator:

    for entry, err := range mf.Entries(fs, discardDeleted) {
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }

    }

or ReadManifest when a slice is needed.

distinct_counts (field 111), which the spec deprecates in every format
version. Writers already omitted the field, so the setter had no effect on
the wire. The Avro field stays on the data file struct, so legacy manifests
that carry it still decode, and writers continue to omit it. The tests now
check both on the struct, and a codec test checks that the entry schema has
no field 111.

This is a breaking change for callers of the removed methods.

subject: fix(io): treat ADLS Gen2 / OneLake directory blobs as directories in blobfs WalkDir (#2180)
body:
* fix(io): walk hierarchical namespace directories in blobfs WalkDir

On ADLS Gen2 accounts with a hierarchical namespace (such as OneLake),
every directory is also stored as a 0-byte blob named after it, with no
trailing slash. gocloud's fs.FS treats any key with an exact object as a
file, so WalkDir stopped at the walk root and reported it as the only
file. Orphan cleanup then listed the table location as its only orphan.

WalkDir now walks a small adapter over the bucket. A key with objects
under it is a directory, and a 0-byte blob named after a child directory
is hidden from listings. Trailing-slash markers on flat stores behave as
before, and the walk makes one listing per directory instead of an
existence check plus a listing.

Fixes #2159

subject: fix(table): validate DV replacement on add (#2054)
body:
Two paths still let a row delta commit more than one live deletion vector
for a single data file:

- Same-delta duplicate DVs on the fast-append path. findReplacedLiveDVs
  collapses added DV references into a set, and when the data file has no
  live DV yet the scan returns nothing; with no RemoveDeletes,
  validateRemovedDeletes (which held the only duplicate-added-DV check)
  never runs, so AddDeletes(dvA, dvB) for one data file committed two live
  DVs. Hoist the duplicate-added-DV check into validateAddedDeletionVectors,
  run unconditionally on every commit path.

- Concurrent first-DV additions across a commit retry. Two writers based on
  a snapshot with no DV for a data file both pass findReplacedLiveDVs. After
  one commits, the other's add-only delta is replayable: doCommit rebuilds
  the manifest list against the refreshed parent but did not re-check DV
  uniqueness, so the retry could inherit the concurrent DV and commit a
  second one. Add validateNoConcurrentReplacedDVs to RowDelta.validate: on
  retry it walks the concurrently committed delete entries and rejects a
  live DV added for a data file this delta also adds a DV for. It is a no-op
  on attempt 0 (no concurrent snapshots), and a removal-carrying delta is
  non-replayable, so there are no removals to reconcile on retry.

Tests: TestRowDeltaFastAppendRejectsDuplicateAddedDVs covers the fast-append
duplicate, and TestRowDeltaRejectsConcurrentFirstDVOnRetry drives the
two-writer retry through the OCC scenario catalog and asserts the retry is
rejected before a second commit attempt.

subject: refactor(table): add Table.ManifestProvider and move inspect onto public (#2151)
body:
* refactor(table): add Table.ManifestProvider and repoint inspect onto public APIs

Introduce a public ManifestProvider (via Table.ManifestProvider) that reads a
snapshot's manifest list through the table's shared, bounded manifest-list cache
and resolves the table FileIO once per provider. It exposes Manifests,
DataManifests, and FS, keeping the internal snapshotManifestSet cache and
sharedSnapshotManifestFSF unchanged behind it.

Manifests and DataManifests return iter.Seq[iceberg.ManifestFile] over the
cache-owned slice. That keeps the no-copy cache hit from #2112 while giving
callers outside the package no way to mutate the shared cache, which a
borrowed []ManifestFile in a public signature could not guarantee.

Repoint the metadata-inspection code off the table package internals it reached
into (the unexported manifestSet / manifestSetWithFSF methods, the fsF field, and
the metadata / metadataLocation fields) and onto public accessors
(Table.ManifestProvider, Table.FS, Table.Metadata, Table.MetadataLocation). The
provider is created once per inspection so the all_* metadata tables still
resolve the backend once and share the manifest cache. AllManifests now fills
its record batches from a reused chunk buffer instead of slicing the manifest
list, with the same batch boundaries; no behavior change.

This leaves the inspection surface depending only on public table APIs, in
preparation for moving it to a dedicated table/inspect package.

* refactor(table): drop ManifestProvider.DataManifests and pin cache sharing

DataManifests had no caller and no test, and it would become permanent
public surface on release. Drop it until a caller needs it; the
data-only view stays available inside the package.

Add a test that reads the same snapshot through two providers from one
Table and checks the manifest list is opened once, so building the
provider without the table's shared cache now fails.

Document that a provider keeps the result of its first FileIO
resolution, error included, so it is meant for one operation and a new
provider is needed to retry.

subject: feat(table,rest): enforce the catalog's scan-planning-mode directive (#2162)
body:
* fix(table): add ScanPlanningDirective() accessor on table

Previously, the table returned by a LoadTable() on a REST catalog did
not have any way of exposing what scan planning mode the catalog is
trying to enforce on this table. In cases where the catalog is enforcing
server-side scan planning, the caller would have to rely on errors
and/or missing files through the Scan() interface, to realize that
server-side scan planning is necessary.

This change exposes a ScanPlanningDirective() function on a table.Table
that exposes this value as returned from LoadTableResponse. If the catalog
is not imposing any particular scan planning mode,
ScanPlanningDirectiveUnknown is returned.

* fix(table): carry scan-planning directive state explicitly

Address review feedback on the ScanPlanningDirective accessor:

- WithScanPlanningDirective now takes (value, ok) so absence is explicit
  and a comma-ok map read can be passed straight through.
- Add WithScanPlanningDirectiveFrom to copy a table's directive verbatim;
  RefreshTableCredentials uses it instead of reconstructing the raw value
  from SavedConfig, which could report the wrong directive for externally
  built tables.
- Drop the positional loadConfig parameter from tableFromResponse; load
  paths pass the directive as a caller option instead.
- Rename ScanPlanningDirectiveUnknown to ScanPlanningDirectiveNone and
  document that it only means "no directive" with a nil error.
- Use a switch over the valid directives.
- Add coverage for Commit, StagedTable, Refresh, CreateTable,
  RegisterTable, and LoadTable followed by a credential refresh.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: fix(catalog): report stale commit requirements as ErrCommitFailed and add commit conformance tests (#2248)
body:
* test(catalog): add table commit tests to the catalog conformance suite

Cover the CommitTable path, which every catalog implements but the suite
did not exercise: create-time properties, property set/remove, schema
evolution, a commit whose requirement went stale under a concurrent
writer, and a commit through a handle to a dropped table.

* fix(catalog): classify failed commit requirements as ErrCommitFailed

SQL, Hive, Glue and Hadoop validated commit requirements locally and
returned the bare requirement error, while REST maps the same case
(409) to table.ErrCommitFailed. A stale writer on those catalogs was
therefore never retried by the commit retry loop, and a commit to a
dropped table did not report ErrNoSuchTable.

Validate requirements through one shared helper that reports a failure
on a missing table as catalog.ErrNoSuchTable and any other failure as
table.ErrCommitFailed. Retries remain opt-in through
commit.retry.num-retries, which defaults to 0.

* test(catalog/rest): run conformance suite against Apache Polaris

against an Apache Polaris server, a second REST implementation alongside
the Java REST fixture. Testing against two servers surfaces client-side
divergences that a single fixture can mask, such as the rename error
mappings fixed in #2165 and #2173.

unaffected. POLARIS_CREDENTIAL and POLARIS_WAREHOUSE are required once
it is enabled. CONTRIBUTING.md documents starting a local Polaris server
with file storage, including the CATALOG_MANAGE_CONTENT grant the client
needs because it requests vended credentials by default.

* test(catalog/rest): move Polaris setup into a script

Address review feedback on the Polaris conformance test:

- Move the bootstrap out of CONTRIBUTING.md into
  internal/recipe/setup-polaris.sh, next to the compose file so CI can
  reuse it. CONTRIBUTING keeps a short pointer.
- The script bounds the readiness wait and prints the container logs if
  Polaris never comes up, fails on a missing token (jq -e) and surfaces
  error bodies (curl --fail-with-body), and replaces its container on
  each run so it can be rerun.
- Explain the readiness override: Polaris refuses to start with FILE
  storage otherwise, since it flags FILE as a severe security risk.
- Require POLARIS_CREDENTIAL to be a client_id:client_secret pair.
- Log which outcome RenameTableToSelf took, so a backend's self-rename
  behavior is visible in a passing run.

subject: fix(catalog/rest)!: make OAuth token refresh context-aware and singleflight (#2265)
body:
AuthHeaderWithContext checked ctx once and then called Token()
synchronously, so a caller blocked on a stalled token endpoint until the
refresh client's Timeout regardless of its own deadline. Concurrent
callers each ran their own refresh in turn behind the token source's
mutex.

Share one in-flight Token call per manager with a singleflight.Group and
let the caller wait for it only until ctx is done. The refresh keeps
running, bounded by the refresh client's Timeout, and its result serves
later callers. AuthHeader goes through the same group.

BREAKING CHANGE: Oauth2AuthManager is no longer comparable. The type has
only unexported fields and pointer-receiver methods, so no caller can
hold two meaningful values to compare.

Signed-off-by: Ilia Demianenko <ilia.demianenko@clickhouse.com>

refactor(io)!: add context to IO.Open and IO.Remove (#2067)
body:
* refactor(io)!: add context to IO.Open and IO.Remove

`io.IO.Open` and `Remove` now take `context.Context`, matching `BulkRemovableIO.DeleteFiles`.
`blobfs.FileIO.Remove` forwards the caller context so deletes honor cancellation/deadlines.
`maintenance.WithCleanupDeleteFunc` now takes `func(context.Context, string) error`.

Breaking change: all `IO` implementations/callers must pass a context, and custom delete callbacks must update their signature.

Part of the v1.0 API cleanup in #2062.

Signed-off-by: laskoviymishka <laskoviymishka@gmail.com>

* fix(io): keep failure cleanup immune to caller cancellation

Moving blobfs Remove onto the caller context made cleanup after a failed
operation fail with it: when the failure was itself a cancellation or a
timeout, the removal was canceled too and files that used to be cleaned
up were left behind on object stores. Before this change Remove ran on
the context captured when the FileIO was built, so a canceled caller
never reached it.

Run those cleanup paths on context.WithoutCancel(ctx), which keeps the
context's values (tracing and similar) but not its cancellation:

- doCommit's deferred removal of orphaned manifest lists
- the hadoop catalog's temp metadata file and version claim removals
- sql removeUncommittedMetadata, which already loaded the filesystem
  without cancellation but removed with the caller context
- the removal of a partially written delete manifest in
  writeDeletedEntries
- the Glue S3 Tables commit rollback

Paths where removal is the requested work (orphan cleanup, PurgeFiles,
expire snapshots' post-commit deletes, drop namespace and drop view)
keep the caller context so they stay cancellable.

Tests use an IO that rejects Remove on a canceled context, as blobfs
does, to check that doCommit and removeUncommittedMetadata still clean
up after a cancellation.

Also reword the IO.Open doc to say implementations may use ctx to bound
the open, since no backend does yet, and drop the comments claiming
every backend ignores ctx, which would go stale once one honors it.

Signed-off-by: laskoviymishka <laskoviymishka@gmail.com>

* refactor(table): thread ctx through the manifest content cache IO

The manifest content cache that landed on main wraps the scan FileIO
with the old context-free Open and Remove, so the merge no longer
built. Give manifestContentCacheIO the context-taking signatures.

Opens of other paths and Remove forward the caller's context. The
cached manifest path keeps using the scan context captured in wrap,
because the manifest readers that call Open have no caller context to
pass and would otherwise drop the scan's cancellation. The cache's
own opens, including the population read and the fallback opens, use
that same context.

Signed-off-by: laskoviymishka <laskoviymishka@gmail.com>

subject: fix(table): pin guarded refs in RollbackToSnapshot and ExpireSnapshots (#2301)
body:
* fix(table): pin guarded refs in RollbackToSnapshot and ExpireSnapshots

Since #2248 the SQL, Glue, Hive and Hadoop catalogs report a failed
commit requirement as ErrCommitFailed, so with commit.retry.num-retries
above zero doCommit retries it and rewrites the commit branch's
AssertRefSnapshotID to the refreshed head. RollbackToSnapshot and
ExpireSnapshots rely on that assertion to detect a concurrent change, so
a stale rollback could discard a peer's append and a stale expiry could
remove snapshots the moved branch still retains. REST was already
affected through 409 responses.

Pin the refs these operations guard, including branches the transaction
staged, using the same mechanism as Transaction.AssertRefSnapshotID.
Pins and the staged updates are now published under one lock, so a
failed apply leaves no pin. A pinned assertion that no longer holds
after refresh fails the commit without spending the rest of the retry
budget.

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

* fix(table): skip guards for a no-op ExpireSnapshots

An ExpireSnapshots call that finds nothing to expire stages no update,
but it still pinned every ref. In a transaction that also appends, the
pin on the commit branch stopped the append from rebasing onto a peer's
commit, so the retry failed instead of succeeding.

Return without adding requirements or pins when there is nothing to
expire, while still rejecting a transaction that has already been
committed.

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

* test: trim pinned-ref test helpers and clarify retry docs

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

* docs: list every built-in catalog in the retry support note

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>

* docs: limit the catalog support note to conflicting requirement failures

Signed-off-by: Harrison Crosse <harrison@crosse.dev>
